cards.explanation: The answer is the men of Hezekiah king of Judah. The text says these are additional proverbs of Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1), and that they were copied by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah (Proverbs 25:1). Somebody had to sit down and copy them all out. I think that took real patience, and I get nervous just carrying a full tray across the kitchen.

The answer is to search it out. "It is the glory of God to conceal a matter and the glory of kings to search it out." (Proverbs 25:2) God conceals a matter, and kings get glory from searching it out. Searching takes effort, friends. I think a little digging is just fine.

The answer is their hearts. "As the heavens are high and the earth is deep, so the hearts of kings cannot be searched." (Proverbs 25:3) That's about as far as you can go in both directions. Nobody gets to the bottom of it.

The word is wicked. "Remove the wicked from the king’s presence, and his throne will be established in righteousness." (Proverbs 25:5) Same as the silver, where you take out the dross first. Clear the wicked out and the throne stands on solid ground.

The answer is righteousness. With the wicked removed from his presence, the king's throne "…will be established in righteousness." (Proverbs 25:5) A throne set on that holds firm. I wish my wobbly baking table could say the same.

The answer is demoted in front of the prince. "…it is better to be told, “Come up here!” than to be demoted in the presence of the prince." (Proverbs 25:7) Getting invited up beats getting sent down, friends. Solomon would rather you wait for the invitation than grab the seat yourself. I think walking back down from the big seat has to be the longest walk there is.

The answer is True. Solomon asks what you'll do in the end "…when your neighbor puts you to shame?" (Proverbs 25:8) That's the risk of bringing something hastily to court, even something you saw with your own eyes. Slow down before you take it that far.

The answer is False. The verse says to argue your case with your neighbor "…without betraying another’s confidence…" (Proverbs 25:9) You can make your argument, but another person's secret isn't yours to spend. Win or lose, that door stays closed.

The answer is a word fitly spoken. "A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver." (Proverbs 25:11) The right word at the right time is a treasure, like gold set in silver. Solomon is talking about what we say, not what we own. I think that's rarer than a perfectly even batch, and I work hard on those.

The word is listening. "Like an earring of gold or an ornament of fine gold is a wise man’s rebuke to a listening ear." (Proverbs 25:12) A listening ear is what makes the rebuke worth wearing. I think a stubborn ear would just leave the jewelry in the box.

The answer is True, friends. "Like the cold of snow in the time of harvest is a trustworthy messenger to those who send him; he refreshes the soul of his masters." (Proverbs 25:13) That's the picture Solomon chooses for a trustworthy messenger. The ones who send him are the ones who get refreshed.

The answer is the man who boasts of gifts never given. "Like clouds and wind without rain is the man who boasts of gifts never given." (Proverbs 25:14) Big talk, lots of promise, and then nothing falls. Clouds without rain are all show. Solomon's point is that a boast means little without a gift behind it.

The answer is False, and the verse says it plainly. "Through patience a ruler can be persuaded, and a gentle tongue can break a bone." (Proverbs 25:15) A gentle tongue has real power. Soft words can do more than you'd think.

The answer is that you vomit it up. "If you find honey, eat just what you need, lest you have too much and vomit it up." (Proverbs 25:16) Not pretty, but honest. Take what you need and leave the rest.
The answer is False. The verse says "Seldom set foot in your neighbor’s house, lest he grow weary and hate you." (Proverbs 25:17) Too many visits can leave a neighbor tired of you. Keep it seldom.

The answer is a man who bears false witness against his neighbor. "Like a club or sword or sharp arrow is a man who bears false witness against his neighbor." (Proverbs 25:18) Three weapons, all for a lie told about a neighbor. Words can hurt like they have an edge.

The word is faithless, friends. "Like a broken tooth or a foot out of joint is confidence in a faithless man in time of trouble." (Proverbs 25:19) You lean on him when you need him most, and he gives out. That's the pain Solomon is describing.

The answer is that he sings songs to it. "Like one who removes a garment on a cold day or vinegar poured on a wound is one who sings songs to a heavy heart." (Proverbs 25:20) Solomon pictures a cold day with the garment gone, and a wound with vinegar poured in. Songs aimed at someone who is hurting just add to the sting. I think sometimes the kind thing is to say less.

The answer is to give him food to eat. "If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat…" (Proverbs 25:21) Solomon says it plainly, with no list of conditions, friends. A hungry enemy is still hungry. Giving the food is the instruction.
The answer is the LORD. The verse says "…and the LORD will reward you." (Proverbs 25:22) That's the line right after the burning coals. Caring for an enemy is something the LORD rewards.

The answer is a backbiting tongue. "As the north wind brings forth rain, so a backbiting tongue brings angry looks." (Proverbs 25:23) A backbiting tongue brings angry looks, the way the north wind brings rain. Talk behind someone's back, and the faces change. Just like the weather, you can see it coming.

The answer is sharing a house with a quarrelsome wife. "Better to live on a corner of the roof than to share a house with a quarrelsome wife." (Proverbs 25:24) A corner of the roof sounds cramped, but Solomon says it's better. He's saying a quarrelsome home is hard to live in. I think constant arguing wears everyone down.

The answer is True, friends. "Like cold water to a weary soul is good news from a distant land." (Proverbs 25:25) Good news from far away refreshes a weary soul the way cold water does. Solomon's picture is a cool drink for someone worn out. I think a cold drink does the same for a tired body.

The answer is False. The verse says the muddied spring or polluted well is "…a righteous man who gives way to the wicked." (Proverbs 25:26) It's the giving way that spoils the water. Standing firm is the opposite picture.

The answer is searching out your own glory. "It is not good to eat too much honey or to search out one’s own glory." (Proverbs 25:27) Solomon puts the two side by side, friends. He says it's not good to eat too much honey. In the same breath, he says it's not good to search out your own glory.

The word is temper. "Like a city whose walls are broken down is a man who does not control his temper." (Proverbs 25:28) Walls keep a city safe, and a man without control of his temper has nothing to hold things back. I've had my own hot moments over burnt batches.
